You are editing the HTML template of a published web page about a Fortress port of microGPT. Read-only sources first, then one file to edit. No commits, no publishing, no git operations, no touching anything under /home/user/fortress except reading.

## Context
The page currently opens its linear-algebra section with the claim that vectors/matrices over the program's `Value` type do not exist in Fortress, so four "carrier" types (`Vec`, `ProbDist`, `Mat`, `KVCache`) had to be built. A later blinded clean-room investigation showed that flat negative was wrong and the true situation is three-way. Read this report in full, it is the authority for every factual change you make:

/home/user/fortress/explorations/libvector-report.md

Summary of what it establishes (verify against the report, cite its sections/probes, do not add claims it does not support):
1. The standard library's own `Vector[\T,n\]`/`Matrix[\T,n,m\]` DO carry `Value` completely (construction, `M v`, `v M`, `M N`, transpose, `u+v`, scaling, `SUM`, runtime-sized shapes), but only by declaring `Value extends Number`, which the specification forbids (`trait Number comprises { RR64 }`; traits.tex:231-235) and which the walk interpreter never checks because it never enables the static checker.
2. The spec-legal route (extending the unsealed `AdditiveGroup`/`MultiplicativeRing`) gets `+ − scale pmul t()` and stops dead at `dot`, `mul`, `rmul`, `lmul`, every top-level operator, and `SUM`.
3. Therefore the page's carriers are the spec-legal route around an unenforced seal, not a substitute for something absent. The correct reading is: the library has the types, the seal is load-bearing, the carriers are what conformance costs.
4. The spec promises `m^T`, `m^k`, `‖m‖` and the library ships none of them (report §6); the page's one-line `^T` therefore fills a library-vs-spec gap, not merely a notation choice.
5. Five smaller defects (report §0 table and §7/§9): array literal needs explicit LHS type (implementation gap), array comprehension is NI (implementation gap), missing `^T ^k ‖·‖` (library gap vs spec), `matrix` factory fills off-diagonals with literal `0` (library bug), `SumReduction.empty() = 0` so empty SUM can't yield a Value (library-design limit).

## The file to edit
/tmp/claude-0/-home-user-fortress/bdff267d-67dc-5bb9-b970-8c3dfaa634b6/scratchpad/pres4-template.html

Three places, minimal edits, preserving the page's voice (plain, exact, no self-praise, no hedging filler):

A. Lines ~160-172, the paragraph beginning "Papers write vectors and matrices". Replace the sentence "None of this exists in Fortress for our Value" with the three-route truth in two or three sentences: library types exist and would carry Value in full, but only through a declaration the spec forbids and the interpreter fails to reject; the legal route dies at the dot product; the carriers are the conforming route. Keep the rest of the paragraph (the forty-nine lines, the rank traits, the summation sign) intact unless a clause now contradicts the correction.

B. Lines ~176-188, the figcaption of the notation sheet. Where it says the spec special-cases postfix `^T` and "We initially declared this impossible; an adversarial review found the sentence and the one-line definition", add that the library itself ships no `^T` (nor `^k`, `‖m‖`) despite the spec promising them, so the one-liner also fills a library gap. One sentence.

C. Lines ~595-607, the ledger table "What the language could and could not say" (columns: the paper writes / the program says / why, classified). Add rows, in the table's existing terse style, for:
   - `W x` over the library's own Vector/Matrix → carriers instead → classify: the seal `Number comprises {RR64}` is spec-mandated and load-bearing (dot/mul/SUM need it); the interpreter's failure to enforce it is an implementation gap; the carriers are the conforming route.
   - `Kᵀ`, `Mᵏ`, `‖M‖` → `^T` defined in one line; others unused → library gap vs spec.
   - `[i ↦ e | i ← …]` array comprehension → not usable (interpreter says not implemented) → implementation gap.
   - the `matrix` factory `else 0` bug and `SumReduction.empty() = 0` may share one row or be omitted if they do not fit the paper-writes/program-says framing; use judgment, keep the table honest.
   Also update the sentence after the table if needed ("Every row is probed, cited, and recorded in the repository's expressiveness review") so that it also points at the libvector report by name (`explorations/libvector-report.md`).

Also search the rest of the template for any other sentence asserting that library vectors/matrices cannot hold `Value` or "do not exist"; grep for "Vector", "Matrix", "carrier", "library" and fix contradictions, but do not rewrite unrelated prose.

## Rules
- Never write any AI model name or identifier into the file.
- No self-congratulation; the page records its own corrections plainly ("we declared X; a blinded probe showed Y").
- Do not modify anything under /home/user/fortress. Do not run git. Do not publish.
- After editing, run `python3 /tmp/claude-0/-home-user-fortress/bdff267d-67dc-5bb9-b970-8c3dfaa634b6/scratchpad/build_pres4.py` (it inlines figures into microgpt-presentation.html in the same directory) and confirm it exits 0. If it fails for reasons unrelated to your edit, report the error verbatim rather than fixing the script.
- Check the HTML you wrote is well-formed (balanced tags in the rows/paragraphs you touched).

## Report
Your final message: a short list of the exact edits made (line ranges, one line each), the build_pres4.py exit status, and any sentence in the report you were unsure how to render. Under 300 words.

1	<!-- Produced by a delegated clean-room research worker, 2026-08-30, on Pavol's
2	     challenge: why does microgpt2 define Vec/Mat instead of using the standard
3	     library's own Vector/Matrix? The worker was blinded: barred from reading
4	     anything in explorations/, briefed only with the goal and build environment.
5	     Probes: explorations/libvector-probes/ (p00-p33 with full transcript). -->
6	
7	# Can the Fortress standard library's own `Vector`/`Matrix` carry a user-defined element type?
8	
9	Clean-room probe, walk interpreter, JDK 25, `FORTRESS_THREADS=1`. Sources: `Specification/**/*.tex`, `Library/*.fss|.fsi`, `ProjectFortress/LibraryBuiltin/*.fss`, `ProjectFortress/src/**`, plus 34 running probes.
10	
11	## 0. VERDICT
12	
13	**YES — fully, for every item on the list, including runtime-chosen dimensions. But only by writing a declaration the specification forbids.**
14	
15	The library's `Vector[\T,s0\]` and `Matrix[\T,s0,s1\]` serve as the working representation for a user element type — construction, indexing, `|v|`, `M v`, `v M`, `M N`, transpose, `u+v`, scaling by a `Value`, `SUM`, set/list comprehensions, in-place mutation, rectangular runtime-sized shapes — provided the program declares:
16	
17	```fortress
18	object Value(data: RR64) extends Number
19	    getter asString(): String = "V(" data ")"
20	    opr +(self, other: Value): Value             = Value(data + other.data)
21	    opr -(self, other: Value): Value             = Value(data - other.data)
22	    opr -(self): Value                           = Value(-data)
23	    opr TIMES(self, other: Value): Value         = Value(data other.data)
24	    opr juxtaposition(self, other: Value): Value = self TIMES other
25	end
26	```
27	
28	**The smallest thing standing in the way is one clause:** `comprises { RR64 }` on `trait Number` (`/home/user/fortress/Library/FortressLibrary.fss:352`, `.fsi:276`). `Value extends Number` is illegal Fortress (`/home/user/fortress/Specification/basic/traits.tex:231-235`; worked counter-example at `:265-275`). The walk interpreter never runs the check: `walk` does not call `setTypeChecking(true)` (`/home/user/fortress/ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/Shell.java:420-424`), the flag defaults false (`Shell.java:1275`), and `StaticChecker.checkCompilationUnit` returns untouched when off (`/home/user/fortress/ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/compiler/StaticChecker.java:166`). The check that *would* fire is `/home/user/fortress/ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/scala_src/typechecker/TypeHierarchyChecker.scala:206-208` — `"Invalid comprises clause: … has a comprises clause but its immediate subtype … is not eligible to extend it."`
29	
30	The seal is genuinely load-bearing, not decorative (§5). The spec-legal alternative — extend the *unsealed* `AdditiveGroup`/`MultiplicativeRing` — gets `+ - scale pmul t()` and stops dead at `dot`, `rmul`, `lmul`, `mul`, and every top-level operator.
31	
32	Five smaller independent defects, three of which bite plain `RR64` just as hard:
33	
34	| # | defect | class | bites RR64? |
35	|---|---|---|---|
36	| A | array literal needs explicit LHS type; no inference | implementation gap | yes |
37	| B | array comprehension `[i \|-> e \| g]` is `NI(…)` | implementation gap | yes |
38	| C | `m^k`, `m^T`, `\|\|m\|\|` promised by spec, absent from library | library gap vs spec | yes |
39	| D | `matrix[\T,n,m\](v)` fills off-diagonals with literal `0` | library bug | latent |
40	| E | `SumReduction.empty() = 0`, so empty `SUM` can't yield a `Value` | library-design limit | n/a |
41	
42	## 1. What ships, what the spec promises
43	
44	`Library/FortressLibrary.fsi:1458-1469` / `.fss:2187-2202`:
45	
46	```
47	trait AnyVector end
48	trait Vector[\T extends Number, nat s0\]
49	        extends { AnyVector, Array1[\T,0,s0\], AdditiveGroup[\Vector[\T,s0\]\] }
50	        excludes { AnyMultiplicativeRing }
51	    opr +(self, v:Vector[\T,s0\]): Vector[\T,s0\]
52	    opr -(self, v:Vector[\T,s0\]): Vector[\T,s0\]
53	    opr -(self): Vector[\T,s0\]
54	    scale(t: T): Vector[\T,s0\]
55	    pmul(v: Vector[\T,s0\]): Vector[\T,s0\]
56	    dot(v: Vector[\T,s0\]): T
57	end
58	```
59	
60	`.fsi:1576-1589` / `.fss:2495-2560` gives `Matrix[\T extends Number, nat s0, nat s1\]` with `scale`, `mul[\nat s2\]`, `rmul`, `lmul`, `t()`. Carriers: `__DefaultVector` (`fss:2204`), `__DefaultMatrix` (`fss:2563`), `TransposedMatrix` (`fss:2571`). Factories: `vector` (`fss:2252-2256`), `matrix` (`fss:2613-2616`). Sparse siblings `SparseVector`, `Csr`, `Csc` (`Library/Sparse.fsi:19-36`) carry the identical `nat` + `Number` shape. Top-level operators at `fss:2258-2281` and `2618-2655`.
61	
62	Two constraints are baked in: **`T extends Number`** and **`nat` dimensions**.
63	
64	Spec:
65	- `Specification/basic/expressions/aggregate.tex:153-156` — "An array of two dimensions **whose elements are a subtype of `Number`** is a matrix." `:165-167` — same for one-dimensional/vector. So the `Number` bound is the spec's own design, not a library accident.
66	- `Specification/basic/trait-parameters.tex:66-94`; the chapter's canonical example is literally `makeVector[\T extends Number, nat s0\]() : Vector[\T,s0\]` (`basic/examples/StatParam.Nat.tex`). Line 80: "These parameters are **instantiated at runtime** with numeric values."
67	- `Specification/basic/traits.tex:231-235` — a `comprises` clause makes its listed traits "**exactly** the traits that immediately extend `T`"; `:265-275` shows `trait ExclusiveMolecule extends Molecule` labelled `(* Not allowed! *)`.
68	- `Specification/basic/operators/opr-overview.tex:56-57, 75-81, 86-90` — norm of "a vector **or matrix**", `e^k` for vectors and square matrices, superscript transpose `^T`.
69	- `Specification/appendices/future.tex:243-246` records the *wish* that `array1[\T extends Number, nat s0\]()` return `Vector[\T,s0\]` by overloading — matching the `(* TODO: fix when Number is covariant. *)` hack actually shipped at `fss:2239-2244`.
70	
71	## 2. Baseline: plain `RR64`
72	
73	### 2.1 Construction — partly broken, not the user type's fault
74	
75	`p01`, `a = [1.0 2.0 3.0 4.0]`:
76	
77	```
78	com.sun.fortress.exceptions.ProgramError: …p01_rr64_vec_construct.fss:7:5:
79	Can't infer element type for array construction
80	```
81	
82	`ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/interpreter/evaluator/LHSEvaluator.java:117-140`: with no declared LHS type the code does not compute the join of element types — it goes straight to `outerType = error(x, evaluator.e, "Can't infer element type for array construction")` (line 140). The comment at `:136-138` shows the join was intended and never written. **Implementation gap.**
83	
84	Sanctioned alternatives work (`p02`):
85	```
86	a: RR64[4]          = [1.0 2.0 3.0 4.0]  -> [0#4][ 1.0 2.0 3.0 4.0 ]   a IS an AnyVector
87	b: Vector[\RR64,4\] = [1.0 2.0 3.0 4.0]  -> [0#4][ 1.0 2.0 3.0 4.0 ]   b IS an AnyVector
88	```
89	
90	The grammar's other escape, static args inside the literal (`ArrayExpr ::= "[" [StaticArgs] RectElements "]"`, `aggregate.tex:28`), is **not implemented** (`p27`):
91	```
92	…p27_literal_staticargs.fss:18:9-50:
93	    Unmatched delimiters "[\" and "]".
94	```
95	
96	Factories (`p03`):
97	```
98	|vector[RR64,4]()| = 4
99	after manual zero fill: [0#4][ 0.0 0.0 0.0 0.0 ]
100	w = vector[RR64,4](2.5)   -> [0#4][ 2.5 2.5 2.5 2.5 ]
101	u = vector[RR64,4](fn i)  -> [0#4][ 10.0 20.0 30.0 40.0 ]
102	u IS an AnyVector
103	```
104	The 0-arg factory does **not** zero-fill: printing it first threw `Access to uninitialized element 3 of array PrimitiveArray[\RR64,4\]` (`FortressLibrary.fss:2206`).
105	
106	Why a literal becomes a `Vector` — `array1` (`fss:2239-2244`):
107	```fortress
108	array1[\T, nat s0\]():Array1[\T,0,s0\] =
109	     typecase __thrower[\T\] of
110	         () -> Number => vector[\T,s0\]()
111	         else => PrimitiveArray[\T,s0\]()
112	     end
113	```
114	*Element-is-a-`Number`* is what turns an array into a vector. This single typecase is the hinge.
115	
116	### 2.2 Indexing/size — works
117	`a[2] = 3.0`, `|a| = 4`, `m[0,1] = 2.0`, `|m| = 4`, `m.sizes = (2,2)` (`p02`, `p08`).
118	
119	### 2.3 Products and transpose — works (`p08`)
120	```
121	m n     = [ 70.0 100.0 / 150.0 220.0 ]      (juxtaposition = matrix product)
122	m DOT n = same         m.mul(n)= same
123	m.t()   = [ 1.0 3.0 / 2.0 4.0 ]
124	m v     = [0#2][ 3.0 7.0 ]     m.rmul(v) = same
125	v m     = [0#2][ 4.0 6.0 ]     m.lmul(v) = same
126	```
127	
128	### 2.4 Elementwise + and scaling — works (`p04`)
129	```
130	u + v = [ 11.0 22.0 33.0 ]   u - v = [ -9.0 -18.0 -27.0 ]   -u = [ -1.0 -2.0 -3.0 ]
131	2.0 u = u 2.0 = u.scale(2.0) = [ 2.0 4.0 6.0 ]
132	u DOT v = u v = u.dot(v) = 140.0    pmul = [ 10.0 40.0 90.0 ]

304	## 5. What the element type must provide — and why the seal is load-bearing
305	
306	### 5.1 Requirement ladder (bisected)
307	
308	| `Value` declares | result |
309	|---|---|
310	| `+`, `TIMES` only, `extends Number` (`p19`) | **fails**: `** bug! MethodClosure asFloat(self:(FortressLibrary.Number & {FortressLibrary.RR64})):FortressLibrary.RR64 …FortressLibrary.fss:355:5-23 has neither body nor def instanceof Method`, raised from `FortressLibrary.fss:381` |
311	| `+`, `TIMES`, **`juxtaposition`**, `extends Number` (`p20`) | **everything works**: `u DOT v = V(140.0)`, `SUM = V(6.0)`, `m w`, `w m`, `m.t()`, `m m`, `m + m`, `scale`, `pmul` |
312	| `+`, `TIMES`, `asFloat`, **no** `juxtaposition` (`p21`) | **silently wrong**: `u DOT v = 140.0`, typecase reports `… u DOT v SILENTLY became an RR64`; then `u.scale(Value(2.0))` dies with `Unification error: … init0 param 2 (v:Value) got arg 2.0:RR64 of type Float` |
313	| no `opr -`, program uses `u - v` (`p28`) | `** bug! MethodClosure asFloat … has neither body nor def` from `FortressLibrary.fss:377` |
314	
315	Why: `Vector`'s methods use `juxtaposition`, not `TIMES` — `fss:2197` `scale = map(fn (v) => t v)`, `:2199` `pmul`, `:2201` `dot(v) = SUM [(i,me_i)<-self.indexValuePairs] me_i v.get(i)`. Without an override, the inherited `Number.opr juxtaposition(self,b:Number):RR64 = asFloat(self) asFloat(b)` (`fss:380-381`) applies — and `asFloat` is *abstract* at `fss:355`.
316	
317	**Minimum viable element type: `extends Number` + `opr +` + `opr TIMES` + `opr juxtaposition`; add `opr -` (binary and unary) if the program uses vector subtraction/negation. `asFloat`, `zero`, `one`, `^` optional — and supplying `asFloat` *without* `juxtaposition` is actively dangerous.**
318	
319	### 5.2 Why the seal cannot be sidestepped
320	
321	`p18` shows the `T extends Number` bound is **not** checked when instantiating `vector[\Value,3\]`: a non-`Number` `Value` yields an object that typecases as `IS an AnyVector`. But `p31` shows the algebra then collapses:
322	```
323	u + v -> Failed to find any matching overload, args = (Value,Value), overload = { … }
324	   raised inside  Library/FortressLibrary.fss:2193  (Vector.opr + 's  e + v.get(i))
325	```
326	The reason is dispatch, not bounds. Inside the library's generic code, `e + v.get(i)` resolves against the *global* overload table; the user's `opr +(self, other: Value)` is a method on a type the library never heard of. The only table entry that can route `(Value,Value)` back to the user's method is an inherited one — `AdditiveGroup[\T\].+(self:AdditiveGroup[\T\],other:T):T` (`fss:330`).
327	
328	So the spec-legal move is to extend the **unsealed** traits `AdditiveGroup[\T extends AdditiveGroup[\T\]\]` (`fss:328`) and `MultiplicativeRing[\T extends MultiplicativeRing[\T\]\]` (`fss:340`) — neither has a `comprises` clause. `p32`/`p33`:
329	
330	**Works** (`p33`):
331	```
332	u + v      = [0#3][ V(11.0) V(22.0) V(33.0) ]
333	u.scale(V) = [0#3][ V(2.0) V(4.0) V(6.0) ]
334	u.pmul(v)  = [0#3][ V(10.0) V(40.0) V(90.0) ]
335	m.t()      = 3x3 diag V(2.0)
336	m + m      = 3x3 diag V(4.0)
337	m.scale(V) = 3x3 diag V(4.0)
338	u - v, -u  (p32)                                   also fine
339	```
340	
341	**Fails, two distinct ways:**
342	
343	1. **Top-level operators enforce the bound.** `p32`, `u DOT v`:
344	```
345	Failed to find any matching overload,
346	args = (__DefaultVector[\Value,3\],__DefaultVector[\Value,3\]), overload = {
347	        …
348	        DOT[\T extends FortressLibrary.Number,nat n\](me:Vector[\T,n\],other:Vector[\T,n\]):T
349	           …/Library/FortressLibrary.fss:2261:1-2262:69
350	        …
351	```
352	The candidate is listed and rejected. Same for `M v`, `v M`, `M N`, `t u`, `u t` — every `opr juxtaposition`/`opr DOT` at `fss:2261-2277` and `2621-2655` carries `[\T extends Number, …\]`.
353	
354	2. **`SUM` casts to `Number`.** `p33`, `u.dot(v)` / `m.rmul(u)` / `m.lmul(u)` / `m.mul(m)`:
355	```
356	…/Library/FortressLibrary.fss:36:13-27:
357	CastError
358	Context: …fss:36:13-27  ->  fss:1120:25-34  ->  fss:2201:46-57  …
359	```
360	`Vector.dot` (`fss:2201`) is a `SUM`; `opr SUM[\T extends Number\]()` is `Comprehension[\T,Number,Number,Number\](fn x => x, SumReduction, cast[\Number\])` (`fss:3041-3042`); `__bigOperator` applies `o.unwrap` at `fss:1121`; `cast[\T\]` throws `CastError` at `fss:36`.

362	**Therefore the seal is exactly the obstacle.** `Value extends Number` is the only declaration that simultaneously (a) satisfies the `T extends Number` bound on top-level operators, (b) survives `SUM`'s `cast[\Number\]`, and (c) makes an array literal become a `Vector` via `array1`'s `() -> Number` typecase.

424	## 9. Failure classification
425	
426	**Library-design choice**
427	- `Vector`/`Matrix` bound to `T extends Number` with `Number comprises { RR64 }` — the spec makes the same choice (`aggregate.tex:153-167`), so it is deliberate. It is the single obstacle.
428	- `SumReduction` monomorphic in `Number` with `empty() = 0` (`fss:3029`).
429	- Scaling overloads typed `(T, Vector[\T,n\])`, so no `RR64 × Vector[\Value\]`.
430	
431	**Library bug**
432	- `matrix[\T,n,m\](v)` off-diagonal integer `0` (`fss:2616`).
433	- `Vector`/`Matrix` methods written with `juxtaposition` while the inherited `Number.juxtaposition` (`fss:380-381`) silently degrades a user element type to `RR64` — `p21` gives a wrong-typed answer with no diagnostic.
434	- No `opr ^` for `Vector`/`Matrix`, no `opr ||…||` for `Matrix`, no `^T` operator — all promised by `opr-overview.tex`.
435	
436	**Implementation gap**
437	- No element-type inference for array literals (`LHSEvaluator.java:117-140`).
438	- `[\StaticArgs\ …]` inside an array literal not parsed (`aggregate.tex:28`).
439	- Array comprehensions unimplemented at two layers (`ExprDisambiguator.scala` has no case; `Evaluator.java:881-887` is `NI`), and no `opr BIG [ ]` in `Library/`.
440	- `comprises` never checked on the walk path (`Shell.java:420-424` + `1275`, `StaticChecker.java:166`); the only checker that would check it (`TypeHierarchyChecker.scala:206-208`) is reachable only via phases that cannot handle this library (`typecheck` → `CompilerLibrary`; `typecheck-old` → errors on `FortressLibrary.fsi` itself).
441	
442	**Spec-design limit**
443	- `nat` dimensions are static parameters (`trait-parameters.tex:69-72`), so a value name can never be a static argument. Mitigated by `NatReflect.reflect`, which the spec anticipates at `trait-parameters.tex:80` and which `NatReflect.fss`'s own comment says "we ought to build in and document in the spec".
444	
445	## 10. Smallest thing standing in the way
446	
447	**One `comprises` clause** — `/home/user/fortress/Library/FortressLibrary.fss:352` (and `.fsi:276`):
448	```fortress
449	trait Number
450	        extends { StandardPartialOrder[\Number\], StandardMinMax[\Number\],
451	                  AdditiveGroup[\Number\], MultiplicativeRing[\Number\] }
452	        comprises { RR64 }
453	```
454	Today a user program can just declare `Value extends Number` and get everything, because the walk interpreter never checks the clause. That is a *bug working in the user's favour*: the program is illegal Fortress (`Specification/basic/traits.tex:265-275`) and would be rejected the moment the type hierarchy checker were enabled on the interpreter path.
455	
456	Principled fixes, smallest first:
457	1. **`comprises { RR64, ... }`** — the spec already provides the ellipsis form for exactly this (`traits.tex:236-238`; legal only in an API). One token in `FortressLibrary.fsi:276` makes every result in §4 legal.
458	2. Failing that, **relax the three bounds that actually bite**: change `[\T extends Number\]` to `[\T extends MultiplicativeRing[\T\]\]` on the top-level `DOT`/`juxtaposition` operators (`fss:2258-2281`, `2618-2655`), and make `SUM`'s unwrap not `cast[\Number\]` (`fss:3042`). Then the spec-legal `extends { AdditiveGroup[\Value\], MultiplicativeRing[\Value\] }` route in `p32`/`p33` becomes complete — and `array1`'s `() -> Number` typecase (`fss:2242`) needs a companion test so literals still become vectors.
459	3. Independently and cheaply: `fss:2616` `else 0` → `else v.zero`.

## github
The GitHub MCP Server provides tools to interact with GitHub platform.

Tool selection guidance:
	1. Use 'list_*' tools for broad, simple retrieval and pagination of all items of a type (e.g., all issues, all PRs, all branches) with basic filtering.
	2. Use 'search_*' tools for targeted queries with specific criteria, keywords, or complex filters (e.g., issues with certain text, PRs by author, code containing functions).

Context management:
	1. Use pagination whenever possible with batches of 5-10 items.
	2. Use minimal_output parameter set to true if the full information is not needed to accomplish a task.

Tool usage guidance:
	1. For 'search_*' tools: Use separate 'sort' and 'order' parameters if available for sorting results - do not include 'sort:' syntax in query strings. Query strings should contain only search criteria (e.g., 'org:google language:python'), not sorting instructions. Always call 'get_me' first to understand current user permissions and context. ## Issues

Check 'list_issue_types' first for organizations to use proper issue types. Use 'search_issues' before creating new issues to avoid duplicates. Always set 'state_reason' when closing issues. ## Pull Requests

PR review workflow: Always use 'pull_request_review_write' with method 'create' to create a pending review, then 'add_comment_to_pending_review' to add comments, and finally 'pull_request_review_write' with method 'submit_pending' to submit the review for complex reviews with line-specific comments.

Before creating a pull request, search for pull request templates in the repository. Template files are called pull_request_template.md or they're located in '.github/PULL_REQUEST_TEMPLATE' directory. Use the template content to structure the PR description and then call create_pull_request tool.

reduction now builds a chain of the binary + declared above — which is exactly the chain Karpathy's own sum() over Value objects builds, so the two tapes have the same shape and the verification compares like with like. Priced honestly: +30% tape nodes (1,384 → 1,802 on the verification config) and +25% seconds per step, with every checked number unmoved to fifteen decimals. backward is the chain rule as eleven lines.

Teaching it linear algebra — the notation is the lesson

Papers write vectors and matrices: W x applies a matrix, q·k measures alignment, Kᵀ transposes. None of this exists in Fortress for our Value — and building it is not overhead to hide but half of what this page teaches. Forty-nine lines teach the language all of it: four carrier types — Vec and ProbDist under a shared rank-1 supertype, then Mat and KVCache — riding the library's own mutually-exclusive rank traits, the trick taken straight from the library's numeric vectors that makes both W x and p V legal at once, then the summation sign itself, and then one-line operators whose definitions are their own index formulas:

Σ, and what "extensible" turns out to mean

The summation sign is the sharpest test of the whole premise, and this page got it wrong once. An earlier draft said Σ was sealed — that the library grants the glyph only to its built-in numbers, so summation over Values had to be a named sum, a word where the paper has a glyph. The claim was challenged, and rather than argue we re-ran the question blind: a worker given the goal and the build environment and nothing else — no access to these notes or to the conclusion being tested — spent twenty-two probes on it. Half the claim survived; the half that broke is the more interesting one, and this

random numbers come from a different generator than Python's? Measured: no — Fortress runs land inside the spread of fifteen differently-seeded Python runs at exactly the rate a sixteenth seed would. What does matter is that Fortress's built-in random() cannot be seeded, so no run can be exactly repeated (the 2012 library ships a seedable Mersenne Twister, wired to nothing — worklist). And there is a deeper story here: reproducible randomness under parallel, order-free execution — exactly Fortress's paradigm — requires generators that can split into independent children. They did not exist when Fortress ended. Two years later, Guy Steele built them for Java: SplitMix (2014), then the LXM family (2021). The language's unmet need became its designer's next research program.

The ladder

This page shows the destination of four verified programs. The same attention block, three ways — every rung passing the same nine-decimal verification before the next was attempted, so the ladder is a controlled experiment in notation with the mathematics pinned:
